title: Same Meal, Double the Price: Hyderabad Man's Bill Shows Why Swiggy Costs More
excerpt: A Hyderabad diner's side-by-side comparison — Rs 230 at Panchakattu Dosa versus Rs 436 on Swiggy for the same meal — has reignited debate over platform fees and inflated menu prices.
body:
• Hyderabad X user @idlebrainjeevi posted a side-by-side comparison on September 13: three items at Panchakattu Dosa in Banjara Hills cost Rs 230 in person but Rs 436 for the same meal on Swiggy — Rs 206 more.
  • The markups were item by item: a dosa priced at Rs 104 in the restaurant was listed at Rs 149 on the app, pongal went from Rs 85 to Rs 115, and filter coffee from Rs 28 to Rs 120.
  • The viral post has reignited debate over platform fees, inflated menu prices and restaurant commissions — and the history of consumer-court pushback against packing charges.

A Hyderabad man's receipt has become the internet's latest proof that ordering in costs far more than dining out. The side-by-side comparison he posted on X showed the same meal costing Rs 230 at the restaurant and Rs 436 on Swiggy — an 89% premium for the same food, delivered to the door.

The X user, @idlebrainjeevi, shared the comparison on September 13, matching items from Panchakattu Dosa in Banjara Hills with the same or similar items listed on Swiggy. According to the restaurant bill he posted, three items came to Rs 219.04 before GST: a Neyyi Kaaram Onion Dosa at Rs 104, Neyyi Pongal at Rs 85 and a Filter Coffee at Rs 28. With taxes, the outlet total was Rs 230, according to DainikNews Live.

The Swiggy listing told a different story. The dosa was priced at Rs 149, the pongal at Rs 115 and a Special Filter Coffee at Rs 120 — with no coupon or discount applied, the cart total stood at Rs 436.

"How will delivery companies, delivery drivers make money then if prices are exactly same? Not possible."

— A social media user, responding to the viral post

Context & Background

The gap comes from several layers of markup. Beyond delivery fees, platform fees and packaging charges, the menu prices themselves are frequently higher on the app than at the counter. Netizens responding to the post pointed to the economics behind that: restaurants pay Swiggy commissions of 25-30% on every order, and many simply raise their app menu prices to recover the cut, according to Curly Tales.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=Ovm2jyNuypM

Others were less charitable. One user wrote that "life was so much better before Swiggy and Zomato," while another claimed even quality and quantity are compromised on app orders. Several said they had stopped ordering through apps altogether — a sentiment that echoes a growing fatigue with the economics of food delivery.

Impact & Analysis

This is not a new complaint — and Indian consumers have taken it to court before. In an earlier Hyderabad case, activist Vijay Gopal challenged a Rs 33 "packing charge" Swiggy had levied on a Rs 216.66 order from KFC; the district consumer court termed the charge an unfair trade practice, fined KFC Rs 50,000 and ordered the amount refunded with interest, according to The Better India.

Separately, a Hyderabad court fined Swiggy Rs 35,000 for misreporting delivery distance to inflate delivery charges, MediaNama reported. And restaurants have pushed back too: reports have noted Bengaluru restaurants planning to boycott Swiggy over commissions and pricing pressure, according to DainikNews Live.

Diaspora Angle

For NRIs visiting family in India — or ordering meals for parents back home — the gap is a familiar sting: a modest local meal, which looks cheap by US or UK standards, nearly doubles once the app's markups stack up. The commission debate is one the diaspora knows well from DoorDash and Uber Eats, which run on the same playbook of platform fees and inflated menus.

What's Next

The platforms are unlikely to lower fees on their own, and regulators have shown little appetite for intervening in menu pricing. For consumers, the practical recourse so far has been the consumer court — which has, at least in Hyderabad, shown it will take packing charges seriously. Until the economics change, the Rs 230-vs-Rs 436 receipt will keep doing the rounds every time the debate flares up again.
